output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile against a background of high premorbid intellectual functioning. Verbal learning and delayed recall are severely impaired (HVLT-R delayed recall 1/12, 2nd percentile; immediate recall 14/36, 6th percentile), with little benefit from recognition testing (discrimination index 3, 4th percentile), consistent with a storage-type encoding deficit rather than a retrieval-based process. Visual memory is also impaired (Rey Complex Figure delayed recall 6/36, 5th percentile) with an intact copy. Confrontation naming is mildly impaired (Boston Naming Test 44/60, 7th percentile) and semantic fluency is mildly reduced, while letter fluency is preserved. Executive function (Trail Making B, letter fluency) and processing speed (Trail Making A) are within normal limits. Geriatric Depression Scale 4/15 (within normal range). Overall profile is consistent with amnestic multi-domain mild cognitive impairment (episodic memory with milder naming and semantic fluency involvement) in an individual of high premorbid ability.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 25/30 and MoCA 21/30 with delayed recall failure not helped by category cues and mild naming loss; husband confirms 14 months of decline; instrumental independence preserved with her own compensatory strategies, which stages the syndrome as mild cognitive impairment
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: The word-finding complaint and the memory lapses must be measured and staged by function before they are attributed to thyroid disease, language-led neurodegeneration or Alzheimer disease [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe storage-type episodic memory deficit (HVLT-R delayed recall 1/12, recognition discrimination 4th percentile) disproportionate to the naming impairment (Boston Naming 44/60), with preserved executive function and processing speed; amnestic multi-domain mild cognitive impairment rather than logopenic primary progressive aphasia
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile, distinguish amnestic from language-predominant MCI, and establish a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: In a highly educated patient whose complaint is word finding, normed testing is what separates an amnestic syndrome with naming involvement from a language-led one [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH 5.8 mIU/L with normal free T4 on levothyroxine (under-replacement, with calcium and iron co-medication that impair absorption); microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia (ferritin 9 ng/mL); B12, folate and homocysteine normal; RPR and HIV non-reactive; no reversible cause sufficient to explain the decline
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Her primary care physician already attributed the symptoms to the thyroid, so thyroid function and the other treatable contributors must be measured on this visit [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral medial temporal atrophy (Scheltens grade 2) with temporoparietal and precuneus cortical thinning; minimal WMH (Fazekas 1); no mass or hydrocephalus
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy pattern, exclude vascular disease, NPH, and mass lesions, and evaluate for posterior cortical changes
action_criteria.rationale: MRI shows whether medial temporal atrophy supports a neurodegenerative cause and excludes vascular, mass and hydrocephalic causes of the decline [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive florbetapir PET (composite SUVR 1.47)
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral, symmetric temporoparietal and posterior cingulate/precuneus hypometabolism with frontal sparing, an Alzheimer-type pattern rather than the frontotemporal pattern of FTD or the left-lateralized temporoparietal pattern of logopenic aphasia
action_criteria.label: Consider FDG-PET if the syndrome remains uncertain after clinical assessment, labs and structural imaging
action_criteria.rationale: When the language complaint keeps a frontotemporal or logopenic syndrome in question, the metabolic pattern helps separate them from an Alzheimer-type pattern [Foster_2007].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the cognitive decline to the mildly elevated TSH and defer the evaluation pending thyroid optimization; a TSH of 5.8 mIU/L with normal free T4 does not explain a 14-month progressive amnestic syndrome with medial temporal atrophy
Do not anchor exclusively on word-finding difficulty as evidence of a primary progressive aphasia without formal neuropsychological testing to characterize the full cognitive profile

Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine as routine treatment for mild cognitive impairment; neither is approved for MCI and the guideline does not support routine use [AAN_dementia_2018].
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from her husband to document the onset, trajectory and effect on daily functioning

Review levothyroxine adherence and timing: take it on an empty stomach at least 4 hours apart from calcium carbonate and ferrous sulfate, then recheck TSH and free T4 in 6 to 8 weeks before changing the dose; a TSH of 5.8 mIU/L with normal free T4 does not explain the cognitive decline [ATA_hypothyroidism_2014].

Investigate the persistent iron-deficiency anaemia (ferritin 9 ng/mL, MCV 74.3 fL despite two years of oral iron): review absorption (omeprazole, calcium taken with iron, vegetarian diet) and refer for gastrointestinal evaluation [BSG_IDA_2021].

Arrange cognitive and functional reassessment in 6 to 12 months and recommend regular exercise (at least twice weekly); explain that no medicine is approved for mild cognitive impairment [AAN_dementia_2018].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].
Assess safety: driving (two longer-than-necessary routes), medication management, finances, and the support available at home
Disclose the diagnosis to the patient and her husband and begin advance care planning, including advance directives and a healthcare proxy

differential.key_features: Word-finding difficulty and naming impairment as the presenting complaint raise lvPPA; however, repetition is intact, there are no phonological errors, and neuropsychology shows a disproportionate episodic encoding deficit (HVLT-R delayed recall 2nd percentile, recognition 4th percentile) with only mild naming loss: an amnestic syndrome, not a language-led one

differential.diagnosis: Reversible cognitive impairment due to hypothyroidism
differential.key_features: TSH was 6.2 mIU/L before referral and the PCP attributed the complaints to it; on this visit TSH is 5.8 mIU/L with a normal free T4 (1.1 ng/dL) on levothyroxine, a degree of under-replacement that does not produce a severe storage-type amnestic deficit or bilateral hippocampal atrophy

differential.diagnosis: Frontotemporal dementia, behavioral or language variant
differential.key_features: No personality change, disinhibition or apathy, and executive function is normal; episodic memory is the dominant deficit and MRI and FDG-PET show temporoparietal rather than frontotemporal involvement; amyloid positivity, when tested, argues against FTLD

Geriatric Depression Scale 4/15 (normal); insidious 14-month progressive course with severe storage-type encoding deficit (near-zero recognition discrimination index) is not characteristic of depressive cognitive symptoms
No visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism, no REM sleep behavior disorder, no cognitive fluctuations described; DLB is explicitly excluded by history and examination

key_clinical_evidence: Word-finding difficulty as a presenting complaint in early Alzheimer disease is common and should not automatically redirect the work-up toward primary progressive aphasia; the distinguishing feature is the severity of episodic memory impairment relative to naming, and the absence of repetition deficits and phonological errors

A TSH of 5.8 mIU/L with a normal free T4 on levothyroxine, taken alongside calcium carbonate and ferrous sulfate that impair its absorption, deserves treatment optimization but does not explain a 14-month progressive amnestic syndrome with hippocampal atrophy; the two conditions coexist

The neuropsychological signature of amnestic Alzheimer disease is a storage-type deficit: severely impaired free recall with little gain from cueing or recognition, as here (HVLT-R delayed recall 2nd percentile, recognition 4th percentile, no benefit from category cues)

Cholinesterase inhibitors are not approved for mild cognitive impairment and are not recommended routinely at this stage; serial assessment and vascular risk management are the evidence-based steps [AAN_dementia_2018]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Persistent mild under-replacement, plausibly from calcium and iron taken with levothyroxine, warrants optimization but cannot account for a 14-month progressive amnestic syndrome with established hippocampal atrophy on MRI; both conditions may coexist
red_herrings.data_point: TSH 5.8 mIU/L with free T4 1.1 ng/dL four months after the levothyroxine dose was increased from 75 to 100 mcg (TSH 6.2 mIU/L before the increase)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the cognitive and word-finding symptoms primarily to undertreated hypothyroidism and defer further dementia workup pending thyroid optimization — as already occurred prior to referral

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The naming deficit is mild relative to the severe episodic memory impairment (HVLT-R delayed recall 2nd percentile, recognition discrimination 4th percentile), and there are no phonological errors or repetition deficits; the profile is amnestic with secondary naming involvement, not lvPPA
red_herrings.data_point: Word-finding pauses, circumlocution, and mild confrontation naming deficit (Boston Naming Test 44/60) as the primary presenting complaint
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a language-variant dementia (primary progressive aphasia, logopenic variant) and order workup targeted at language rather than episodic memory

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The Geriatric Depression Scale score is 4/15 (normal range) and she denies low mood; a storage-type encoding failure with no cueing benefit and hippocampal atrophy on MRI is not the effortful retrieval pattern of depression-related cognitive impairment
red_herrings.data_point: Family history of 'depression and memory problems' in mother who died at 74 without a formal evaluation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Interpret the cognitive symptoms as late-life depression (pseudodementia) mirroring the mother's undifferentiated presentation

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Priya Venkataraman is a 67-year-old right-handed retired professor of comparative literature who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her husband for evaluation of progressive word-finding difficulty and episodic memory lapses over the past 14 months. The patient herself initially attributed the word-finding trouble to 'retirement rust,' noting that she no longer gave lectures or engaged in academic writing, which she had done daily for 35 years. Her husband first became concerned approximately 14 months ago when he observed her pausing mid-sentence during dinner conversations, reaching for words she would previously have produced effortlessly. She has increasingly resorted to circumlocution and approximations during conversation. Over the past year, she has also begun repeating questions within the same sitting, sometimes asking the same question three to four times within an hour. Approximately eight months ago, the family noticed she was forgetting recent conversations entirely — her son would describe an event over the phone that she had no recall of by the following day. She missed two scheduled doctor's appointments about six months ago; since then she has kept a wall calendar and set phone alerts, has missed none, and still manages her own calendar, correspondence and the household bills, more slowly than before. Her husband has not needed to take over any of these tasks. She continues to drive to familiar locations, though her husband has noted she takes longer routes than necessary on two occasions; there have been no accidents and she has never become lost. She was able to complete her grocery shopping with a list but requires the list, whereas previously she shopped from memory. Her book club participation has become strained; she reports losing the thread of novels she is reading and has had difficulty following plot discussions. Of note, her levothyroxine dose was increased from 75 mcg to 100 mcg approximately four months ago after a TSH of 6.2 mIU/L was found on routine labs; her primary care physician had attributed her subjective complaints partly to the borderline TSH at that time and deferred further workup pending thyroid optimization. Her husband reports no personality change, disinhibition, or apathy. She has no visual hallucinations, no gait difficulties, and no episodes of unexplained falls. She denies depressed mood, hopelessness, or anhedonia; she describes feeling frustrated and embarrassed about the word-finding difficulty but remains engaged and motivated. She has had no headaches, seizures, fever, weight loss, or focal neurological symptoms.

neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No grasp, snout, or palmomental reflexes. No signs of parkinsonism. Mild pallor of conjunctivae bilaterally consistent with known mild anemia.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin normal bilaterally. No dysmetria or intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact. No truncal ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus or diplopia. Visual fields full to confrontation in all quadrants. Facial sensation intact bilaterally to light touch and pinprick. Face symmetric at rest and with volitional movement. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally to finger rub. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue protrudes midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength normal bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady, normal stride length and base. Tandem gait performed without difficulty. Romberg negative. No festination or freezing.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and month and year; gives the date as two days prior. Language: spontaneous speech is fluent but notable for frequent word-finding pauses, particularly for low-frequency nouns; patient uses circumlocution (e.g., 'the thing you use to cut paper' for 'scissors'). Repetition intact. Comprehension intact. Reading and writing intact. No paraphasic errors. MMSE 25/30, losing points on delayed recall (1/3 words at 5 minutes with no benefit from category cues), serial sevens (two errors, starting at 93), and orientation (date). MoCA 21/30, losing points on delayed recall (0/5), naming (2/3), serial subtraction (2/3), abstraction (1/2) and orientation (date). Animal fluency: 12 in 60 seconds (mildly reduced for education). No frank aphasia, apraxia, or neglect on bedside testing.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. No cogwheel rigidity. Strength 5/5 in all extremities bilaterally. No pronator drift. No rest tremor, postural tremor, or action tremor. No myoclonus.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No jaw jerk.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration (128 Hz tuning fork felt for 8 seconds at great toes bilaterally), and joint position sense in all extremities. No cortical sensory deficits (graphesthesia and stereognosis intact).
